archetype.name: Playoff Team (firepower-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose top-heavy forward group and elite top pair out-shoot and out-score nearly everyone, held back from contender form by goaltending that has gone from a strength to a liability and a record that trails its goal margin.

report.headline: Elite attack, leaky backup net: a top-five differential sitting fourth in the Central
report.take:
Colorado's season so far comes down to one strong engine and one weak link. The engine is an offense that scores 4 goals a game, third in the league and 0.8 above the league rate. It is built on volume: 30.6 shots a game, third in the league. The puck stays on their sticks at 5-on-5 too, with a 53% CF % and a .532 xGF %, both top-seven marks. Nathan MacKinnon has 30 points in 18 games, Martin Necas has 23, and Cale Makar (21 points) and Devon Toews (+13) are ranked fourth and third on the defensemen's tab. That is why the forwards grade an A and the blueline an A-. The Goal Diff / GP of 0.89 ranks fifth in the league.

The weak link is the crease, and it is the biggest change from last year. The 2025-26 team that finished first on the site and allowed the fewest goals got 34.3 goals saved above expected. This year's group sits at -5.1, 27th in the league, and the defense has slid to 13th in goals against. It is not evenly spread. Mackenzie Blackwood is fine at .901 and +1.0 GSAx. Scott Wedgewood's five starts at .867 and -5.6 GSAx are worse on their own than the whole team's number. The blowout losses in the last ten, 2-6 at Nashville and 2-7 at Columbus, are the kind of nights that pile up when the backup gets shelled.

What the numbers hide runs both ways. The offense is riding a 13.1% shooting rate, 1.5 points above the league. The 5-on-5 PDO of 103.5 is entirely a shooting story, because the team's save % is exactly league average at .891. Artturi Lehkonen's 12 goals on 38 shots is the clearest example of finishing that will cool. Against that, the record is running behind the goals. Pts vs Goal Diff is -2.4, 28th in the league, which is why a team with a top-five margin is fourth in its own division at 10-6-2. Over a season those two effects tend to cancel. Slower scoring should be offset by better luck in close games.

Where does that leave them? The pace of 100 points is a fair middle estimate. It is below last year's 121 and in line with the 102-to-109 seasons before that. The 5-on-5 play is good but no longer dominant, with xGF % down from .569 to .532. A return toward last year's level needs the goaltending to get back to roughly average and the defense to stop leaking production to centers. The talent at the top makes them a safe playoff team either way.

strengths.title: Volume-driven top-three offense
strengths.body: Colorado scores 4 goals a game, third in the league, on 30.6 shots a game, also third. The finishing will cool from 13.1%. The shot volume and a top-seven xGF % are repeatable, so this should remain a top-five attack even after regression.

strengths.title: MacKinnon and an elite top pair
strengths.body: MacKinnon's 30 points lead a forward group graded A. Makar and Toews rank fourth and third on the defensemen's tab, with xGF % near .585 each. The rest of the blueline is ordinary: Kulak and Burns sit outside the top 120. The A- grade leans heavily on two players, but those two are proven drivers.

strengths.title: Record trails the goal margin
strengths.body: At -2.4, Pts vs Goal Diff is 28th in the league. The standings undersell a team with the fifth-best differential per game. Close-game results usually even out, so some points should flow back.

concerns.title: Goaltending collapse from last season
concerns.body: Team GSAx has fallen from 34.3 to -5.1, 27th in the league, and the defense has slipped from first to 13th in goals against. Blackwood has been slightly above expected. Wedgewood's .867 in five starts is the damage. The fix is fewer Wedgewood starts, or better ones from him, and that is the single biggest lever on the season.

concerns.title: Shooting luck inflating the attack
concerns.body: A 5-on-5 PDO of 103.5 with league-average goaltending means the finishing is doing the lifting. All-situations shooting is 1.5 points above the league, and Lehkonen has 12 goals on 38 shots. Expect the goals to come down even if the chances don't.

concerns.title: Centers are scoring freely against them
concerns.body: Opposing centers have out-produced their own averages against Colorado, and the team ranks 28th at holding them down. Centers account for a larger share of the points allowed than the league norm. That points to the middle of the defensive structure rather than the goalies alone.

trend.note: A strong October margin has narrowed into a 5-4-1 last ten with lopsided results both ways, including 2-7 and 2-6 losses alongside 5-2 and 4-0 wins. The last five (3-1-1) steadied the points but scored and allowed fewer goals than the season rates.

weekAhead.headline: Three road games against teams Colorado out-plays
weekAhead.body:
All three games are in the East and on the road, with a day off between each, so the starter can plausibly carry the week. None of the three opponents matches Colorado's 5-on-5 profile. Toronto is 26th in xGF % and allows 29.4 shots a game. Ottawa and Montréal both run power plays in the bottom five. The likely risk is special teams in Toronto and a hot Montréal goalie.

Montréal's 11-3-3 is the most dangerous-looking record, but it leads the league in Pts vs Goal Diff. Its play is closer to Colorado's than its record suggests, and slightly below. Two of three points-wise games look winnable on process. Montréal is a coin flip leaning Colorado if the goaltending holds.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume vs Toronto's weak blueline
keyMatchups.body: Toronto's defensemen grade D-, it allows the sixth-most shots a game, and it owns only 45.9% of the 5-on-5 expected goals. Colorado's shot-heavy attack should tilt the ice. The catch is Toronto's special teams: a fifth-ranked power play and fourth-ranked penalty kill can steal games a team loses at even strength.

keyMatchups.title: Ottawa's wings are exposed
keyMatchups.body: Ottawa holds centers well, sixth in the league, but ranks 26th against wingers. Wingers take 45.8% of the points scored against it. That is an opening for Lehkonen, Landeskog and Schwartz more than for MacKinnon. Ottawa's 13.2% power play also means Colorado's 78.2% kill should face little pressure.

keyMatchups.title: Montréal's record outruns its play
keyMatchups.body: Montréal leads the league in Pts vs Goal Diff and gets strong goaltending (6.2 GSAx). Its xGF % of .523 is just below Colorado's. It is also soft against centers, ranking 21st, which suits MacKinnon, Necas and Kadri.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal. With no back-to-backs, a three-game Blackwood week would test whether the goaltending problem is really a backup problem.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the scoring to drift down from 4 a game as the shooting percentage and Lehkonen's finishing normalize. Expect the points to catch up to the goal margin as the close-game luck evens out. Those roughly offset, which is why a final total around the 100-point pace is the center of the range. The upside case is goaltending. Blackwood is already above expected, and if he takes most of the starts, team GSAx should climb back toward average. That would lift the defense from 13th toward the top ten and push the club toward 105-plus.

The downside is a thin blueline behind Makar and Toews and continued leakage to opposing centers. Those would keep goals against near the league rate once the finishing cools. Either way, the top-end talent and a top-seven 5-on-5 share make a playoff spot the strong likelihood. A division title will depend on the crease more than the attack.

projections.stat: Goals scored / game, rest of season

swingFactors: Blackwood's share of starts and Wedgewood's save %
How far the 13.1% shooting rate cools
Health and minutes of Makar and Toews

confidence.note: 18 games is a small sample, but shot and possession shares are stable and the luck signals point in opposite directions.
